concept.title: Escher Staircases in Algebra: Infinite Ascending Chains That Loop Back
concept.concept_description: An Escher staircase is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... that nevertheless has I_1 as an element of the infinite intersection. This seems impossible — how can an infinite ascending chain loop back to the beginning? But in the ring of integer-valued polynomials Int(Z), the chain I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z} is strictly ascending (I_n strictly contained in I_{n+1}) yet the intersection of all I_n is {0}, which contains the zero polynomial that is also in I_1. Conjecture: Every non-Noetherian ring contains an Escher staircase, and the 'height' of the Escher effect (measured by the Krull dimension gap) is a new ring invariant. For Int(Z), the Escher height is infinite (the chain never stabilizes). For Z[x_1, x_2, ...], the Escher height equals the number of variables. For the p-adic integers Z_p, there is NO Escher staircase (Z_p is a DVR, hence Noetherian). Test: prove that Int(Z) has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Prove that k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n. Compute the Escher height for the ring of all algebraic integers. Impact: a new invariant for non-Noetherian rings that measures how far a ring is from being Noetherian — the algebraic equivalent of Escher's impossible architecture.

concept.title: Knots That Think: Cognition as Braiding in Category Theory
concept.concept_description: Model a cognitive process as a finite word over the Artin generators σ_i (i ∈ Fin n) of the braid group B_n, where each σ_i contributes +1 to the writhe and each σ_i⁻¹ contributes –1. Define the writhe of a word as the sum of its signed contributions. Prove that the writhe is invariant under the braid relations (the Reidemeister moves) σ_i σ_j = σ_j σ_i for |i‑j|>1 and σ_i σ_{i+1} σ_i = σ_{i+1} σ_i σ_{i+1}, thereby establishing a well-defined braid invariant that can be used to compare cognitive equivalence classes without circular reasoning.
concept.mathematical_framing: The brain's connectome is a braid: neurons fire in sequences that interleave like strands of a braid group. Formalize this: a cognitive process is an element of the braid group B_n where n is the number of brain regions. Two cognitive processes are equivalent if their braids are related by Reidemeister moves (cognitive equivalence). Conjecture: The Jones polynomial of a cognitive braid is invariant under cognitive equivalence and encodes the information content of the thought. A thought with Jones polynomial V(t) = 1 is a trivial thought (equivalent to no thinking). A thought with V(t) = -t^2 + t + 1 is a creative thought (it contains a trefoil knot — the simplest non-trivial braid). The information content of a thought is log(|V(e^{2pi i/3})|), which measures the quantum dimension of the braid. Test: compute the Jones polynomial of braids representing simple cognitive processes (linear reasoning: trivial braid, creative insight: trefoil, confused thinking: figure-eight knot) and verify that the quantum dimension correlates with subjective ratings of thought quality. Impact: thinking IS braiding. The topology of your thoughts determines their quality. Creative insights are literally knotted.
concept.lean_guess: Define cognitive braids: each brain region is a strand, each neural firing sequence is a crossing. A cognitive process is an element of B_n (braid group on n strands). Two thoughts are equivalent if related by Reidemeister moves. Define thought quality Q(braid) = log(|V_braid(e^{2pi i/3})|) where V is the Jones polynomial. Prove Q is a braid invariant. Prove: trivial braid has V = 1 so Q = 0 (trivial thought). Trefoil has V = -t^2+t+1 so Q = log(|V(e^{2pi i/3})|) = log(sqrt(3)) > 0 (creative thought). Figure-eight has Q = log(2) (confused thought with maximum entanglement). Test: compute Jones polynomials for braids B_3 representing simple cognitive processes and rank by Q.

+`σ_i⁻¹`. -/
+def wordToBraid {n : ℕ} (w : List (Fin n × Bool)) : BraidGrp n :=
+  QuotientGroup.mk (FreeGroup.mk w)
+
+/-- The writhe (signed crossing count) of a word: `+1` per positive crossing,
+`-1` per negative crossing. -/
+def wordWrithe {n : ℕ} (w : List (Fin n × Bool)) : ℤ :=
+  (w.map (fun p => if p.2 then (1 : ℤ) else -1)).sum
+
+/-
+The braid-group writhe homomorphism, applied to the interpretation of a word,
+recovers the word's signed crossing count.
+-/
+theorem writhe_wordToBraid {n : ℕ} (w : List (Fin n × Bool)) :
+    writhe n (wordToBraid w) = Multiplicative.ofAdd (wordWrithe w) := by
+  unfold writhe wordToBraid;
+  unfold wordWrithe; erw [ PresentedGroup.toGroup ] ;
+  erw [ QuotientGroup.lift_mk ] ; induction w <;> aesop;
+
+/-
+The concrete trefoil word `σ₀ σ₀ σ₀` interprets to `σ₀³` in `B_{n+1}`.
+-/
+theorem wordToBraid_trefoil {n : ℕ} :
+    wordToBraid [((0 : Fin (n + 1)), true), ((0 : Fin (n + 1)), true),
+        ((0 : Fin (n + 1)), true)]
+      = (sigma (0 : Fin (n + 1))) ^ 3 := by
+  rfl
+
+/-
+The signed crossing count never exceeds the number of firing events, because
+each event contributes at most `+1`.
+-/
+theorem wordWrithe_le_length {n : ℕ} (w : List (Fin n × Bool)) :
+    wordWrithe w ≤ (w.length : ℤ) := by
+  convert List.sum_le_card_nsmul _ _ _ using 1;
+  rotate_left;
+  exacts [ by infer_instance, by infer_instance, 1, by rintro x hx; rw [ List.mem_map ] at hx; obtain ⟨ p, hp, rfl ⟩ := hx; split_ifs <;> norm_num, by simp +decide ]
+
+/-
+The writhe of the trefoil braid `σ₀³` is `3`.
+-/
+theorem writhe_trefoil {n : ℕ} :
+    writhe (n + 1) ((sigma (0 : Fin (n + 1))) ^ 3) = Multiplicative.ofAdd (3 : ℤ) := by
+  have h_writhe_sigma : ∀ (n : ℕ) (i : Fin (n + 1)), writhe (n + 1) (sigma i) = Multiplicative.ofAdd (1 : ℤ) := by
+    intro n i; exact writhe_sigma i

+          ((0 : Fin (n + 1)), true)]).length = 3 := by
+  exact ⟨ wordToBraid_trefoil, rfl ⟩
+

+`σ₀³` consists entirely of positive crossings: a minimal cognitive realization of a

+crossing.

+false in `B_{n+1}` once `n ≥ 1`, since braid relations allow rearrangements; hence we

+-/
+theorem trefoil_min_all_positive {n : ℕ} (w : List (Fin (n + 1) × Bool))
+    (hw : wordToBraid w = (sigma (0 : Fin (n + 1))) ^ 3) (hlen : w.length = 3) :
+    ∀ p ∈ w, p.2 = true := by

+  rcases w with ( _ | ⟨ p, _ | ⟨ q, _ | ⟨ r, _ | w ⟩ ⟩ ⟩ ) <;> simp_all +decide [ wordWrithe ];

+  -- is positive.  Each `if` contributes at most `1`, and the three contributions sum
+  -- to `3`, so each must equal `1`, i.e. each Boolean component is `true`.

+    (by_contra h
+     simp only [Bool.not_eq_true] at h
+     simp only [h] at h_writhe
+     split_ifs at h_writhe <;> omega)

## 1. Quantum thought dimension `log |V(ζ)|`

Evaluation point: `ζ = e^{iπ/3} = 1/2 + (√3/2)·i`, a primitive **sixth** root of
unity, satisfying `ζ² = ζ − 1`, `ζ³ = −1`, `ζ⁶ = 1`, `ζ⁻¹ = 1 − ζ`.

We use the genuine Jones polynomials (Laurent polynomials in `t`):

| thought        | knot | Jones `V(t)`                    | `V(ζ)`   | `|V(ζ)|` | info `log|V|` |
|----------------|------|---------------------------------|----------|----------|----------------|
| linear/trivial | `0₁` | `1`                             | `1`      | `1`      | `0`            |
| creative       | `3₁` | `-t⁻⁴ + t⁻³ + t⁻¹`              | `-√3·i`  | `√3`     | `½ log 3 ≈ 0.549` |
| confused       | `4₁` | `t⁻² - t⁻¹ + 1 - t + t²`        | `-1`     | `1`      | `0`            |

Hand computations (all reproduced and *proved* in Lean):

* Trefoil: `ζ⁻⁴ = ζ²`, `ζ⁻³ = 1`, `ζ⁻¹ = 1 − ζ`, giving
  `V(ζ) = 1 − 2ζ = −√3·i`, so `|V| = √3`.
* Figure-eight: `ζ⁻² = −ζ`, `ζ² = ζ − 1`, giving `V(ζ) = −1`, so `|V| = 1`.

### Counterexample hunt
The brief conjectured the figure-eight ("confused thinking") is topologically
rich. **Counterexample found:** at `ζ` its information is exactly `0`, identical
to the trivial thought. This is not an artifact of the evaluation point — it is
the Lickorish–Millett phenomenon `|V_K(e^{iπ/3})| = (√3)^{d}`, with `d` the
`Z/3`-rank of `H₁` of the double branched cover:
* trefoil → `L(3,1)`, `H₁ = Z/3`, `d = 1` → `√3`;
* figure-eight → `L(5,2)`, `H₁ = Z/5`, no 3-torsion, `d = 0` → `1`.

The brief's alternate point `e^{2πi/3}` (primitive **cube** root) also collapses
the trefoil to `|V| = 1`; hence the faithful choice `e^{iπ/3}` is used.

A cognitive process is a braid word (list of signed generators). Writhe = sum of
signs. Small cases:

| process            | writhe | length | note                    |
|--------------------|--------|--------|-------------------------|
| `[]`               | `0`    | `0`    | base case               |
| `[σ₀, σ₀⁻¹]`       | `0`    | `2`    | charge 0, nonzero cost  |
| `[σ₀, σ₀, σ₀]`     | `3`    | `3`    | trefoil, tight          |
| `[σ₀,σ₀]++[σ₀⁻¹]`  | `1`    | `3`    | additivity: `2+(−1)=1`  |

Since each event moves the running sum by `±1`, `|writhe| ≤ length`; hence a
thought of net charge `k` needs `≥ k` firing events. The trefoil word shows the
bound is tight (`k = length = 3`).

(quantum dimension of the `Z/3` sector) and the golden ratio / Fibonacci numbers

Five self-contained, falsifiable conjectures arising from this cycle's finding

## 1. The Golden Thought: creative capacity grows at rate `log φ`

Model a train of thought as a sequence of braiding moves on a chain of Fibonacci
anyons, whose fusion spaces have dimensions equal to consecutive Fibonacci
numbers. The creative capacity of an `n`-step thought is the logarithm of its
fusion-space dimension, which should equal `n · log φ` for the golden ratio
`φ = (1+√5)/2`, with the space itself of dimension `F_{n+1}`.

**The key insight is** that a thought's capacity is not a fixed number but an
*exponential resource* whose growth rate is a single universal constant, the
golden ratio, distinguishing an unbounded creative sector from the quantized,
bounded `√3` sector seen in the trefoil.

**Why now?** The exact `½ log 3` value for the trefoil shows the quantum-dimension
measure is sharp and computable; extending from a single knot to a growing
anyonic chain is the natural next scale, and the Fibonacci recurrence makes the
growth rate exactly pinnable rather than merely estimated.

## 2. Double-cover homology decides which thoughts are visible

For a knot `K`, the modulus of its Jones polynomial at `e^{iπ/3}` equals
`(√3)^d`, where `d` is the number of independent `Z/3` cycles in the double
branched cover of `K`. Conjecture: across the twist-knot and two-bridge families,
a thought carries positive information exactly when `d > 0`, and this can be read
off from a single congruence on the knot's determinant.

**The key insight is** that "does this thought carry information?" is not
topologically mysterious — it is governed entirely by three-torsion in a single
homology group, reducing a hard invariant to an arithmetic congruence.

**Why now?** The figure-eight's surprising collapse to zero information is exactly
the `d = 0` case; recognizing this pattern turns an isolated anomaly into a
predictive, testable classification across an infinite family.

Net topological charge (writhe) forces a tight lower bound on the number of
firing events realizing a thought, but it is blind to how strands interleave.
Introduce a second measure — the minimal number of adjacent swaps needed to
achieve the thought's permutation of brain regions — and conjecture that the true
firing cost is at least the maximum of the two, with explicit families where each
term dominates.

**The key insight is** that cognitive cost has two irreducible sources, an
abelian one (net directed charge) and a non-abelian one (reconfiguration of
regions), and neither alone captures the difficulty of a thought.

**Why now?** The writhe bound is already sharp for the trefoil; its very sharpness
exposes that it says nothing about permutation complexity, motivating the second,
orthogonal invariant precisely where the first saturates.

## 4. Compound thoughts add their information

When two thoughts are joined end-to-end (a connected sum of their knots), their
quantum-dimension information should add exactly: a compound of `k` independent
creative insights carries `k · ½ log 3`, and gluing on a trivial thought changes
nothing.

**The key insight is** that the information of a thought is an *extensive*
quantity — it scales linearly with the number of independent insights it
contains, so creativity accumulates additively rather than saturating.

**Why now?** Having a clean closed value for a single creative insight makes the
additivity law directly checkable, and it predicts a linear ladder of information
levels that can be compared against graded notions of thought complexity.

apart all thoughts below a fixed complexity.

figure-eight proves this by mimicking triviality at one point — but a short

**Why now?** This cycle produced an explicit collision (figure-eight vs. trivial

digits admitting a factorization `v = x * y`, where `x` and `y` (the *fangs*)
each have half as many digits as `v` and **together use exactly the multiset of
digits of `v`**, subject to the classical side condition that `x` and `y` do not
both end in `0`.  The smallest example is `1260 = 21 · 60`.

The heart of the definition is a purely combinatorial constraint: the digits of
`x` and `y`, taken together, are a permutation of the digits of the product
`x * y`.  We isolate this as `DigitPermFactorization` and derive three
structural obstructions that every such factorization must satisfy.  These are
the arithmetic "silver bullets" that any candidate vampire pair must survive.

## Main results

* `VampireNumbers.castingOutNines` — **casting out nines for factorizations**:
  a digit-permutation factorization forces `x * y ≡ x + y [MOD 9]`,
  equivalently `(x-1)(y-1) ≡ 1 [MOD 9]`.
* `VampireNumbers.fang_not_one_mod_three` — a sharp corollary: neither fang can
  be `≡ 1 (mod 3)`.  This is a genuine sieve that eliminates candidate pairs.
* `VampireNumbers.digit_length_additive` — a digit-permutation factorization
  forces the product to have the *maximal* possible length
  `len(x*y) = len(x) + len(y)`, i.e. the multiplication loses no leading digit.

We then package the classical definition (`IsVampirePair` / `IsVampire`) and
verify `1260 = 21 · 60` as an honest instance, showing the three obstructions in
action.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

Hypothesis (Hypothesizer):  We floated several conjectures.
  (H1) The stated density claim "vampire numbers have density → 1/√n in
       [10^{2n},10^{2n+1}]" is ill-posed: 1/√n → 0, so it asserts vanishing
       density, contradicting the intended reading of "density approaches 1".
       We flag it as false-as-stated and do not pursue it.
  (H2, SURVIVED) Casting out nines must constrain any digit-permutation
       factorization: since a number is ≡ its digit sum (mod 9) and the fang
       digits are a permutation of the product's digits, `x*y ≡ x+y (mod 9)`.
  (H3, SURVIVED, SURPRISING) The mod-9 identity `(x-1)(y-1) ≡ 1 (mod 9)` forces
       both `x-1` and `y-1` to be units mod 3, hence *no fang is ≡ 1 (mod 3)* —
       a one-line sieve rejecting ~1/3 of candidate factors.
  (H4, SURVIVED) The permutation condition forbids "carry shrinkage": the
       product must have length exactly len(x)+len(y).

Experiment (Experimenter):  Base cases confirm H2/H3/H4: for 1260 = 21·60,
  21·60 = 1260 ≡ 21+60 = 81 ≡ 0 (mod 9); 21 ≡ 0, 60 ≡ 0 (mod 3), neither ≡ 1;
  len(1260)=4 = len(21)+len(60)=2+2.  Mathlib supplies
  `Nat.modEq_nine_digits_sum` (`n ≡ (digits 10 n).sum [MOD 9]`), which is the
  exact fuel for H2.

Analysis (Analyst):  See sibling `Analysis` blocks; H2–H4 are all true and
  proved.  H1 is false as literally stated.  The multiset formulation (rather
  than `List.Perm`) is what makes the sum/length transfers a one-line
  `congrArg`.

Critique (Critic):  None of the three main theorems is `decide`/`native_decide`;
  each transports a Mathlib modular/multiset lemma through the permutation
  hypothesis.  The `1260` instance uses `decide` only for the concrete finite
  digit computation, not for a universally-quantified claim.

Synthesis (PI):  Casting out nines + the mod-3 unit obstruction + length
  additivity form a compact, reusable "bestiary sieve" for arithmetic monsters.
-/

namespace VampireNumbers

open Nat

/-- A **digit-permutation factorization**: the base-10 digits of the product
`x * y`, as a multiset, are exactly the digits of `x` together with the digits
of `y`.  This is the combinatorial core of every "vampire-style" definition. -/
def DigitPermFactorization (x y : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (↑(Nat.digits 10 (x * y)) : Multiset ℕ)
    = (↑(Nat.digits 10 x) : Multiset ℕ) + (↑(Nat.digits 10 y) : Multiset ℕ)

/-- The digit sums add: this is the multiset condition read through `sum`. -/
theorem digit_sum_additive {x y : ℕ} (h : DigitPermFactorization x y) :
    (Nat.digits 10 (x * y)).sum = (Nat.digits 10 x).sum + (Nat.digits 10 y).sum := by
  have := congrArg Multiset.sum h
  simpa using this

/-- **Casting out nines for digit-permutation factorizations.**
If the digits of `x` and `y` together permute the digits of `x * y`, then
`x * y ≡ x + y [MOD 9]`.  Equivalently `(x-1)(y-1) ≡ 1 (mod 9)`.

*Analysis:* the whole argument is `n ≡ digitsum(n) (mod 9)` applied three times,
glued by the additive digit-sum identity above. -/
theorem castingOutNines {x y : ℕ} (h : DigitPermFactorization x y) :
    x * y ≡ x + y [MOD 9] := by
  have hsum := digit_sum_additive h
  have hxy := Nat.modEq_nine_digits_sum (x * y)
  have hx := Nat.modEq_nine_digits_sum x
  have hy := Nat.modEq_nine_digits_sum y
  calc x * y ≡ (Nat.digits 10 (x * y)).sum [MOD 9] := hxy
    _ = (Nat.digits 10 x).sum + (Nat.digits 10 y).sum := hsum
    _ ≡ x + y [MOD 9] := (hx.add hy).symm

/-- The mod-3 shadow of casting out nines. -/
theorem castingOutThrees {x y : ℕ} (h : DigitPermFactorization x y) :
    x * y ≡ x + y [MOD 3] :=
  (castingOutNines h).of_dvd (by norm_num)

/-- **The mod-3 unit obstruction.**  In any digit-permutation factorization,
*neither fang is congruent to `1` modulo `3`*.  Indeed if `x ≡ 1 (mod 3)` then
`x*y ≡ x+y (mod 3)` collapses to `y ≡ 1 + y`, i.e. `0 ≡ 1 (mod 3)`.

*Analysis:* casting the mod-3 identity into `ZMod 3` turns the obstruction into
a two-element linear contradiction. -/
theorem fang_not_one_mod_three {x y : ℕ} (h : DigitPermFactorization x y) :
    x % 3 ≠ 1 ∧ y % 3 ≠ 1 := by
  have h3 := castingOutThrees h
  have hcast : (x : ZMod 3) * y = (x : ZMod 3) + y := by
    have := (ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff _ _ _).mpr h3
    push_cast at this
    exact this
  have key : ∀ a b : ℕ, (a : ZMod 3) * b = (a : ZMod 3) + b → a % 3 ≠ 1 := by
    intro a b hab ha
    have hA1 : (a : ZMod 3) = 1 := by
      have h' : (a : ZMod 3) = ((a % 3 : ℕ) : ZMod 3) := by rw [ZMod.natCast_mod]
      rw [h', ha]; simp
    rw [hA1, one_mul] at hab
    have hcontra : (0 : ZMod 3) = 1 := by linear_combination hab
    exact absurd hcontra (by decide)
  exact ⟨key x y hcast, key y x (by rw [mul_comm, add_comm]; exact hcast)⟩

/-- **Length additivity / no carry shrinkage.**  A digit-permutation
factorization forces the product to attain the maximal possible number of
digits: `len(x*y) = len(x) + len(y)`.  Generically `len(x*y)` could be one less
(when the top digits multiply without carrying into a new place); the
permutation condition rules this out.

*Analysis:* multiset cardinality equals list length, so this is `congrArg
Multiset.card` applied to the defining equation. -/
theorem digit_length_additive {x y : ℕ} (h : DigitPermFactorization x y) :
    (Nat.digits 10 (x * y)).length
      = (Nat.digits 10 x).length + (Nat.digits 10 y).length := by
  have := congrArg Multiset.card h
  simpa using this

/-! ## The classical vampire number and a worked instance -/

/-- A **vampire pair**: `v = x * y` is a `2k`-digit number whose fangs `x, y`
each have `k` digits and together permute the digits of `v`, with the classical
"no trailing zeros in both fangs" side condition. -/
structure IsVampirePair (v x y : ℕ) : Prop where
  factor : v = x * y
  even_length : Even (Nat.digits 10 v).length
  equal_fang_length : (Nat.digits 10 x).length = (Nat.digits 10 y).length
  perm : DigitPermFactorization x y
  not_both_trailing_zero : ¬ (x % 10 = 0 ∧ y % 10 = 0)

/-- `v` is a **vampire number** if it has some vampire factorization. -/
def IsVampire (v : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ x y, IsVampirePair v x y

/-- `1260 = 21 · 60` is a vampire number. -/
theorem isVampire_1260 : IsVampire 1260 := by
  refine ⟨21, 60, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · norm_num
  · decide
  · decide
  · show (↑(Nat.digits 10 (21 * 60)) : Multiset ℕ) = _
    decide
  · decide

/-- The three obstructions in action on the smallest vampire number,
each obtained from the general theorems rather than by direct computation. -/
theorem obstructions_1260 :
    (21 * 60 ≡ 21 + 60 [MOD 9]) ∧ (21 % 3 ≠ 1 ∧ 60 % 3 ≠ 1)
      ∧ (Nat.digits 10 (21 * 60)).length
          = (Nat.digits 10 21).length + (Nat.digits 10 60).length := by
  have hperm : DigitPermFactorization 21 60 := by
    show (↑(Nat.digits 10 (21 * 60)) : Multiset ℕ) = _
    decide
  exact ⟨castingOutNines hperm, fang_not_one_mod_three hperm,
    digit_length_additive hperm⟩

end VampireNumbers

# Future Directions — A Bestiary of Arithmetic Monsters

These conjectures grew directly out of the casting-out-nines analysis of
digit-permutation factorizations and the binary-digit-sum bridge.

## 1. A complete residue sieve for fangs

**Conjecture.** For every digit-permutation factorization `v = x·y` (digits of
`x` and `y` together permute the digits of `v`), the residues of the fangs are
confined to an explicit lattice modulo `9`: writing `u = x-1`, `w = y-1`, one has
`u·w ≡ 1 (mod 9)`, so `(x mod 9, y mod 9)` lies in a set of exactly `6·6/…`
admissible pairs, and analogous congruences hold modulo every repunit-related
modulus `10^k − 1`.

The key insight is that casting out nines is only the first member of an infinite
family: a number is congruent to its digit sum not just modulo `9`, but modulo
`99`, `999`, and every `10^k − 1` after grouping digits into blocks of length `k`.
Each modulus yields an independent multiplicative constraint on the fangs, and
their intersection should pin candidate fang residues to a vanishingly small
fraction of all pairs.

Why now? The base case (`mod 9`) is now a proved theorem, and the block-digit
generalization uses the same one-line multiset-to-sum transfer, so the whole
tower is within reach and would turn "hunting for vampires" into solving a small
system of congruences.

## 2. The mod-3 obstruction forces a density ceiling

**Conjecture.** Because neither fang of a digit-permutation factorization can be
`≡ 1 (mod 3)`, the number of vampire numbers below `N` is at most a constant
times `N / (log N)` for large `N`; more precisely the fang-pair count is bounded
by the number of pairs avoiding the residue class `1 (mod 3)`, giving an
unconditional upper density that tends to `0`.

The key insight is that a purely local congruence obstruction (proved here) has a
global counting consequence: eliminating a fixed positive fraction of factor
residues at every scale multiplies through to a genuine density bound, with no
analytic input required.

Why now? The local obstruction `fang_not_one_mod_three` is established, so the
remaining step is a clean combinatorial counting argument over admissible residue
classes rather than any hard analytic number theory.

## 3. No carry shrinkage characterizes the fang length split

**Conjecture.** A composite `v` with `2k` digits is a vampire number **iff** it
factors as `v = x·y` with `x, y` each of length `k` and `len(x·y) = len(x)+len(y)`
(no leading-digit loss) together with the digit-multiset condition; moreover the
"no carry shrinkage" condition alone already rejects a positive proportion of
balanced factorizations.

The key insight is that the digit-permutation hypothesis secretly encodes a
*metric* statement — the product must occupy the maximal number of decimal places
— so length additivity is not a corollary but an equivalent reformulation that
can be checked before any digit comparison.

Why now? Length additivity is now proved as a necessary condition; testing
whether it is also sufficient-modulo-permutation is a finite, decidable check at
each length and would give the first "length-first" vampire-detection algorithm.

## 4. Binary submultiplicativity and the complexity of monsters

**Conjecture.** For all `x, y`, the binary digit sum satisfies
`s₂(x·y) ≤ min(y·s₂(x), x·s₂(y))`, and among numbers with a fixed number of
binary `1`-bits, vampire numbers are exactly those whose fang factorization
nearly saturates this bound; consequently vampire numbers are "binary-simple"
relative to random composites of the same size.

The key insight is that multiplication is repeated addition, so subadditivity of
the digit sum upgrades to submultiplicativity, converting a base-2 complexity
measure into a testable constraint on base-10 factor structure.

Why now? Submultiplicativity is now a proved bridge theorem linking two
previously separate digit theories, so the next step — measuring how tightly real
vampire numbers approach the bound — is a concrete experiment on an already-formal
inequality.

## 5. Ghost numbers are governed by a forbidden-digit last-place law

**Conjecture.** A *ghost number* (a product `v = x·y` sharing no decimal digit
with either factor) must satisfy a rigid final-digit law: the last digit of `v`
equals `(last digit of x)·(last digit of y) mod 10` yet must avoid the digit sets
of `x` and `y`, and this alone forces the count of ghost numbers below `N` to be
`o(N)`, i.e. density zero.

The key insight is that the last decimal place is a closed multiplicative system
on ten symbols, so a disjointness constraint there propagates outward and starves
the supply of admissible products as the digit count grows.

Why now? The digit-multiset machinery built for vampires transfers verbatim to
disjointness conditions, so the ghost density-zero claim can be attacked with the
same multiset-to-residue transfer already validated for casting out nines.

concept.title: Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them
concept.concept_description: What if the topology of a space depended on who is observing it? Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X. Two observers o1, o2 agree on an open set U if U is open in both T(o1) and T(o2). The phantom number of (X, T) is the minimum number of observers needed to determine the topology: if U is open in every T(o) that contains a point x, then U is a neighborhood of x in the 'real' topology. Conjecture: Every second-countable space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with at most 2 observers (the real topology is the intersection of two phantom topologies). Moreover, every non-metrizable space requires at least 3 observers. The intuition: the real topology is what ALL observers agree on, and phantom topologies are what individual observers see.
